SHOW THE WORK

Honest about the limits.

Compare detector versions on transparent synthetic examples.

This is a small development check, not a real-world accuracy claim.

The original 30 cases now form a regression set: their failures informed v2. Another 24 cases were written before the v2 changes by the same AI-assisted author; they are not an independent benchmark. Neither set is T-Mobile’s dataset.

Original v1 baseline: 9/16 scams flagged; 1/10 legitimate messages flagged. V2 expands coverage; review-level warnings are not definitive scam verdicts.

Choose a set and run it to inspect each result.

What’s behind the result?

PausePoint uses explainable, deterministic rules primarily for English message text, plus limited Spanish transfer and code-request patterns. Strong cues can raise a warning; weaker cues invite independent verification. No warning means “uncertain,” never “safe.”

It cannot authenticate senders, inspect websites, detect every scam, or understand every language and context. Obfuscation and subtle social engineering may evade it. T-Mobile’s supplied classifier and dataset have not been integrated because the files are not yet available.

TRANSPARENCY FIRST

Your words stay here.

Message analysis happens in this browser using rules. Message text is not sent to a server, stored in browser storage, or included in downloaded plans. “Clear all” removes it from the app’s current view.

The hosting service may receive standard page-request metadata. Following an external resource opens a different site with its own privacy policy.

A prototype with boundaries

This app does not authenticate a sender, block messages, submit reports, or contact anyone for you. It can miss scams and flag legitimate text. Guidance is general and based on linked U.S. consumer resources.

No sponsor affiliation or endorsement is implied. AI coding assistance was used to develop this project; no generative AI runs during analysis.
